job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at six, take the bus to a small civil engineering consultancy in Sheffield, and spend the day checking drainage drawings for housing estates. I share a rented house with two other people and my room costs me 380 a month. By evening I'm usually on the sofa, opening another letter from the student loan people and trying not to do the sums.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of the job, and what's the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when a drawing I checked turns into an actual road with actual drains. The worst part is the debt. I have less than a month of spending saved, and nobody in my family can top that up, so one broken laptop would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, nothing to panic about, and I'd go back to work. My colleagues already complain that the checking software flags nonsense, so I'd just tell them it's another tool that half works. Online I probably wouldn't say anything, I don't use those sites much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes little for me, and that's the problem. My pay is low and the debt isn't going anywhere. If AI is hype then I'm just a graduate on entry money in a town with very few engineering openings, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my contract, because this was the only offer I got after sending out 60 applications. I'd put 50 a month into a savings account until it reaches one month of rent, and ask my boss for the chartership training they promised. I won't touch the AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared, just tired, because the worry I have already is the money, and a quiet world doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put 50 a month aside. Where does that money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From not buying lunch. I'd take sandwiches in a box and drop the one night out a week with my flatmates, which I'll miss, but a bus pass is 70 and I can't cut that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our drainage checker, Mr Bell, who's 61 and still draws by hand beside the screen. If the software got much better he'd be asked to retire first, and I'd be next in line after him because I'm the newest.

say: It's mostly hype, and I'd tell colleagues it's **another tool** that half works.
I'd stay out of online arguments and keep my head down at work.
think: My **debt** and thin pay worry me more than any machine does.
With so few engineering jobs nearby, losing this contract would be hard to recover from.
do: Keep the **graduate contract** and ask about chartership training this year.
Save **50 a month** by packing lunches until I hold one month of rent.
Skip AI tools and keep checking drawings the way I was taught.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, because the money pressure is already here.
S0.quote: I'd keep my head down and keep my contract, because this was the only offer I got after sending out 60 applications.
fieldNote: He's **anxious** before AI comes up, and the debt is the real driver.
Public line is calm and dismissive of AI; private worry is about the **contract**.
Refuses to use AI tools, which he treats as a point of principle and also of habit.

steps.text: Pack sandwiches and drop the weekly night out
Move 50 a month into a savings account
Keep the contract and ask for the chartership training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what unions have warned about for years: change is fine, but who gets the savings? I'd tell my friends we need rules on what firms can replace, and sick pay and retraining paid by the company, not by us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is the kind that goes first. Checking drawings against standards is exactly the checking and planning work the card talks about. The firm could hire two graduates fewer next year and no one would notice from the outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether our firm has a union rep or an engineers' association and join it before anything is announced. I'd also sit with the senior engineer on site visits, because site work is hands-on and I'd like my job to include more of it. I still wouldn't use the AI checker unless my boss orders me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and angry together. Angry because the people who make the software will get rich and I'll be the one explaining to my landlord why rent is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the checker unless ordered. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my place in the queue. The graduates who use it will look quicker, and my manager counts speed. But I'd rather be slow and right, and I'm not convinced the tool is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, because she worries enough already about me and the loan. I'd say I'm joining a group of engineers, and I'd keep the rest to myself.

say: Change is fine, but **firms must share** the savings and pay for retraining.
I'd push friends to back **unions** and clear rules on what can be replaced.
think: Checking drawings is **thinking work** that software takes first, and I'm the newest hire.
I fear the firm simply **hires fewer** graduates and nobody calls that a layoff.
do: Join an **engineers' association** or union rep before any announcement.
Ask to join senior engineers on **site visits** for more hands-on experience.
Avoid the AI checker unless my boss orders it.
feel: **Uneasy and angry**, because gains go to software owners while I face rent.
S1.quote: The people who make the software will get rich and I'll be the one explaining to my landlord why rent is late
fieldNote: Progressive framing: blames **firms** and software owners, wants collective answers.
Resistance to AI is a principle but may cost him on **speed**.

steps.text: Join an engineers' union or association before layoffs start
Shadow the senior engineer on site visits twice a month
Write to my local councillor about retraining rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a joke. Nobody can prepare in two years, not firms, not councils, not a person with a loan. I'd be loud about it online, to be honest, saying governments need a basic income plan right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm done. A first-year drainage checker is exactly what a thinking machine replaces, and the robots to build the road come three years later, which does not help me during the three years in between. I'd be out of work with loan payments due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving into the small account and keep every pound in cash. I'd ask my landlord whether I could move to a cheaper room, and I'd go to my parents' town and sign up for whatever the council offers. I'd also join the protest the unions organise, because I'd have nothing to lose and time to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, in a flat way, like standing at the top of stairs in the dark. I wouldn't sleep much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep every pound in cash. Why not the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the loan payments come out of pay and stop if I earn under the limit, I think. Cash lets me eat. I'd rather owe more later than have an empty fridge now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who still wants to study engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the friend to wait a year before paying fees. A degree is a bet on ten years of work, and nobody can promise me that now.

say: Two years is **far too fast**, and governments need a basic income plan now.
I'd shout about it online and tell friends to **back the unions**.
think: A first-year checker is **exactly the job** a thinking machine replaces.
The robots arrive three years later, which does nothing for me in between.
do: Hold savings in **cash** and stop extra payments into the loan.
Ask my landlord for a **cheaper room** within three months.
Join union protests and sign up for any **council retraining** offered.
feel: **Scared** and flat, with little sleep, because there is no time to prepare.
S2.quote: A degree is a bet on ten years of work, and nobody can promise me that now.
fieldNote: Most distressed of his five answers; expects to **lose the job**.
Blames **governments** and employers for no plan; strongly union-minded.
Practical but defensive: **cash** first, loan second.

steps.text: Keep every spare pound in cash instead of paying the loan
Move to a cheaper room or back to my parents' town
Join the union protest outside the council office
Sign up for any council retraining or support offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but not zero, and the point is to use it to force policy. I'd tell friends and workmates to push for retraining funds and for firms to say honestly what jobs they plan to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd have maybe three working years left in this line, and I'd want to be out of drawing-checking before then. The debt would be partly paid by 2031 if I'm careful, but not fully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get chartered, because that's a licence a machine doesn't hold, and to move toward site work. I'd ask the firm to put me on a hands-on project. I'd also pay the loan down hard while pay lasts, even if it means eating cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier than with two years. I'd still feel the clock, but it's a clock I can work against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said chartership, a licence a machine doesn't hold. Is that certain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it isn't. I'm guessing the law keeps a human signing off safety, but I don't know. It's my best bet, and I'd ask the institution what they think before spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our site foreman, Rashid, who has been kind to me. He'd tell me straight which tickets matter, and he doesn't talk down to me like some of the office staff do.

say: Five years is **short but usable**, and we should force firms to say what they'll cut.
I'd tell friends to demand **retraining funds** now.
think: I'd have about **three working years** left in drawing-checking before it dries up.
The debt would only be **partly paid** by 2031 even if I'm careful.
do: Get **chartered** in the first two years, since a licence may need a human.
Ask for a hands-on **site project** with the foreman.
Pay the loan down hard and eat cheaply.
feel: **Steadier** than with two years, though I still feel the clock.
S3.quote: I'd use the first two years to get chartered, because that's a licence a machine doesn't hold, and to move toward site work.
fieldNote: **Time** gives him a plan, so he becomes more active and less angry.
Uncertain whether **chartership** will protect him, and says so.
Turns to a **foreman** for trusted advice rather than managers.

steps.text: Sit the chartership exams within two years
Put every bonus and overtime payment against the loan
Ask the firm for a place on a site project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to fix things if we start now. I'd tell people to treat this like climate change: act early, plan together and make companies pay into a fund for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels long, and I'd be 32. I could pay off the loan and train in something hands-on, like site management or tunnelling, where robots lag. Still, I'm not sure that world has a fair deal for people like me, even if there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and chip at the loan for three years. Then I'd study part-time for a site management qualification in the evenings, paid by my firm if they'll agree. I'd also vote in every election and join my union branch, because rules matter more than my own plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Ten years is a long time to carry worry, even if it's a smaller worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure the deal would be fair. What would make it fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If firms that replace engineers pay a share into retraining and early pensions. If they keep the savings, I'd get to 32 with a new qualification and nowhere to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your firm for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time off to study. It costs them four hours a week, and I'll give them back loyalty for it. If they refuse, I'll know what they think of graduates.

say: Ten years is enough if we **start now**, like acting on climate.
Companies should pay into a **workers' fund** as they replace jobs.
think: At 32 I could clear the loan and move to **hands-on work** where robots lag.
I doubt the deal will be **fair** for people like me.
do: Keep the job and pay down the loan for **three years**.
Study part-time for **site management**, asking the firm to fund it.
Vote and join my **union branch** to push for fair rules.
feel: **Calmer**, though ten years is a long time to carry worry.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time to carry worry, even if it's a smaller worry.
fieldNote: The slowest scenario eases his panic but not the **debt** pressure, so mood stays anxious.
Wants **fairness** enforced by rules, not goodwill.
Sees hands-on **site management** as a safer long-term path.

steps.text: Pay a fixed 120 a month toward the loan for three years
Take an evening site management course asked of the firm
Vote and campaign for a workers' retraining fund
Attend my union branch meetings every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. No savings, a loan and no one to fall back on means I couldn't survive a gap of even a few months. What would help is a retraining grant I could use while unemployed, and rules that make firms say early what jobs they plan to cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't lazy or unrealistic. Most of us did what we were told: studied hard, took a loan and took the first offer. Now we're asked to be calm about a machine.

headlineQuote: Most of us did what we were told: studied hard, took a loan and took the first offer.
portrait: Femi, 22, is a top-of-the-class civil engineering graduate in his first job at a small consultancy in **Sheffield**.
He carries **heavy debt**, shares a rented house, has under a month of money saved and gets no family help.
Progressive and union-minded, he blames firms and software owners rather than the technology itself.
He avoids AI tools out of habit and principle, and checking drawings is work software takes first.
He is anxious in most worlds, **alarmed** if AGI comes in 2028, and turns to chartership and site work when given time.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries him most, because there would be no time to get out of debt or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining grant** he could use while out of work, plus rules making firms warn staff early before cutting jobs.
